questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of cost most often actually breaks a multi-cloud initiative a year or two in?
options: The operational cost of running two of almost everything, paid by the people who keep both environments working, secure, and understood
The one-time cost of signing the second provider's contract
The cost of the logo design for a dual-cloud architecture diagram
The cost of renaming internal documentation to mention both providers
questions.explain: Raw infrastructure spend on a second provider gets attention up front, but the ongoing operational tax on tooling, skills, security, and monitoring is what typically breaks the initiative's economics over time.

questions.q: Why doesn't Terraform's ability to target more than one cloud eliminate the duplicated-tooling cost?
options: Terraform cannot be used with more than one provider at all
Terraform only works with on-premises infrastructure
Because each provider's services behave differently in practice, so pipelines and policy tooling still need real, separate engineering per provider even when the authoring tool is shared
Terraform requires a separate paid license for every additional cloud provider
questions.explain: A shared IaC tool helps, but 'equivalent' services across providers rarely mean 'identical' in behavior or defaults, so pipelines, policy-as-code, and cost reporting still need provider-specific engineering work.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a team running two clouds needs deep expertise 'twice,' even though core concepts like compute, storage, and networking are similar everywhere?
options: Because certifications expire twice as fast when an engineer holds two of them
Because cloud providers forbid employees from working across more than one platform
Because the concrete, provider-specific implementation details that matter during an incident don't transfer between providers, even though the underlying concepts do
Because every engineer is legally required to specialize in exactly one cloud
questions.explain: The concepts transfer, but the specific details that matter when something breaks are provider-specific, so the organization effectively needs that depth of knowledge twice, which is a real hiring and training cost.

questions.q: Why is 'just configure the second cloud the same way' described as an underestimate of the real security and monitoring cost?
options: Because Azure and AWS use identical configuration screens
Because identity and access models like Microsoft Entra ID and AWS IAM are built on genuinely different concepts, so a security policy must be re-thought, not just re-typed, for the second provider
Because security policies never need to be written down
Because monitoring tools are free on every cloud provider by default
questions.explain: Azure's and AWS's identity and access models differ in underlying concepts, not just UI, so re-creating a security policy on a second provider is real design work, not a copy-paste exercise — and the same applies to building a coherent monitoring view.

questions.q: What are the two real options the lesson gives for handling observability across two cloud providers?
options: Disable monitoring on the second provider entirely
Only monitor cost, never performance or security
Wait for an incident before setting up any monitoring
Maintain two native monitoring stacks in parallel, or pay for a third-party aggregator that unifies the view at its own licensing and integration cost
questions.explain: Running two clouds means either operating each provider's native observability tooling separately or adopting a centralized third-party aggregator — both are additional, ongoing costs a single-cloud setup never pays.
